c.tagline: A sliver of coral where the runway doubles as Main Street.

taxi.color: No official taxi fleet; unmarked private cars
taxi.fareNote: There are no metered taxis; a small number of private cars and pickup trucks give informal, negotiated flat-fare rides, usually arranged through guesthouses.

emergency.note: Medical facilities are very basic; serious cases require medical evacuation to Fiji or Australia/New Zealand, so travel insurance with medevac cover is strongly advised.

hood_desc: The commercial and administrative core of the atoll, wrapped around the airport runway, main wharf and government offices; best for travelers who want to be steps from arrivals and departures.
A busy central village around the Tuvalu Co-operative Society store and market stalls; suits travelers who want easy access to shops, banks and eateries.
Home to Princess Margaret Hospital and several government ministries, a slightly quieter stretch just off the runway; good for longer-stay visitors, officials and aid workers.
The atoll's most populous village, a mix of family compounds and small guesthouses along the lagoon side; suits travelers wanting an everyday residential feel.
A laid-back northern village known for church life and lagoon views, popular with visitors seeking a quieter pace away from the airport bustle.

water.note: Water comes from rainwater catchment and wells with contamination risk; use bottled or boiled water.

sys.n: Informal shared pickup trucks/vans (no fixed routes or schedule)

transit.pay: There is no ticketed public transit system; informal shared trucks and private vehicles are paid in cash with a negotiated flat fare, and most residents and visitors get around on foot, bicycle, or rented motorbike along the single main road.
transit.hours: No fixed schedule; informal transport and errands mostly happen during daylight hours (roughly 6am-9pm).
transit.note: Funafuti's entire road network is a single road of about 10 km running the length of Fongafale islet, so walking, cycling, and motorbike rental (about $10/day) are the main ways to get around.

transit.m: Walk to Vaiaku town centre (5-10 min)

tip.r: Tipping is not part of local custom in Tuvalu and is not expected in restaurants, guesthouses, or for other services.

food.name: Pulaka
food.desc: Swamp taro grown in hand-dug pits, boiled or mashed with coconut cream. The heritage staple, now scarce as saltwater creeps into the pits.

places.name: Funafuti Market
places.note: Morning stalls sell cooked root crops beside fish and rice; most reliable place to find real pulaka.

places.name: Filamona Moonlight Lodge
places.note: Guesthouse dining room plates pulaka and fish for guests; ask the kitchen a day ahead.

places.name: Vaiaku Lagi Hotel restaurant
places.note: The island's main hotel dining room and the easiest sit-down spot for local root crops.

food.name: Coconut crab (uu)
food.desc: Huge land crab, usually simply boiled or grilled and eaten with coconut cream. A special-occasion food, harvested carefully, never an everyday plate.

places.name: Vaiaku Lagi Hotel restaurant
places.note: Serves coconut crab when it comes in; supply is seasonal and limited, so ask ahead.

places.name: Filamona Moonlight Lodge
places.note: Family kitchen will prepare crab for guests when local fishers bring it in.

food.name: Grilled reef and lagoon fish
food.desc: Tuna, wahoo, parrotfish or trevally straight off the boats, grilled over coals with lime and salt. The most common fresh meal on the atoll.

places.name: Funafuti Market
places.note: Fishers sell the morning catch here and nearby stalls grill it to order at lunchtime.

places.name: Vaiaku Lagi Hotel restaurant
places.note: Catch of the day is the safest bet on the menu, with lagoon views from the terrace.

places.name: Roadside grills along the airstrip
places.note: Evening stalls set up once the runway clears, grilling fish and skewers for locals.

food.name: Palusami
food.desc: Young taro leaves parcelled up and baked in thick coconut cream until silky, sometimes with fish or corned beef tucked inside. A Sunday and feast-day staple.

places.name: Funafuti Market
places.note: Sold pre-wrapped in leaf parcels on busy market mornings; buy early, it goes fast.

places.name: Filamona Moonlight Lodge
places.note: Home-style cooking; palusami turns up on the guest table around Sundays and feast days.

food.name: Fekei
food.desc: Sticky sweet pudding of grated taro or pandanus cooked down with coconut cream and cut into squares. The classic Tuvaluan dessert at gatherings.

places.name: Funafuti Market
places.note: Home cooks bring trays of cut fekei and other coconut sweets to the morning stalls.

places.name: Fongafale community hall feasts
places.note: Fatele nights and church feasts are where fekei is made in quantity; visitors are often welcomed.

food.name: Rice, tinned fish and corned beef
food.desc: With almost no arable land, daily eating leans on shipped-in rice, flour and tinned meat, often fried with onion and served over rice.

places.name: Fusi Cooperative store
places.note: The main island store; stock swings with the supply ship, which shapes what everyone eats.

places.name: Small cafes near the airstrip
places.note: Simple counters doing rice plates, fried chicken and tinned-meat dishes at low prices.

food.name: Kaleve (coconut toddy)
food.desc: Sweet sap tapped from the flower spathe of a coconut palm at dawn and dusk, drunk fresh and cool. Toddy cutting is a daily island craft.

places.name: Funafuti Market
places.note: Bottles of fresh morning toddy turn up at the stalls; best drunk the same day.

places.name: Filamona Moonlight Lodge
places.note: Hosts can point you to a toddy cutter or bring a bottle in for guests.

food.name: Pi (green coconut water)
food.desc: A young drinking nut split open with a machete, the water cold and lightly sweet, the soft jelly scooped out after. The default thirst-quencher here.

places.name: Funafuti Market
places.note: Piles of drinking nuts opened on the spot for a few coins; cheapest drink on the atoll.

places.name: Vaiaku Lagi Hotel restaurant
places.note: Serves whole drinking nuts alongside the usual soft drinks if you are not near the market.

landmarks: Funafuti Conservation Area
A protected marine park of turquoise lagoon waters, coral reefs, and uninhabited islets teeming with seabirds and marine life, perfect for snorkeling and picture-postcard atoll scenery.
Funafuti International Airport Runway
The atoll's improbable centerpiece, this single airstrip doubles as the community's social hub, where locals play volleyball, kids fly kites, and evening strolls unfold between flights.
Tuvalu Philatelic Bureau
A quirky must-visit for collectors, this small government office sells Tuvalu's famously colorful postage stamps, a surprising source of national revenue and pride.
Funafuti Lagoon
The vast, calm turquoise lagoon enclosed by the atoll's ring of islets is the visual signature of Tuvalu, ideal for swimming, kayaking, and watching spectacular sunsets.
Tepuka Islet
A postcard-perfect uninhabited sandy islet within the conservation area, fringed with palms and reachable by boat, offering some of the best snorkeling in Tuvalu.
Fongafale Islet War Relics
Rusting World War II-era American military wreckage and remnants scattered along the main islet are haunting reminders of Funafuti's role as a Pacific airbase in the 1940s.
Tuvalu Government Building and Parliament House
The modest but dignified seat of the world's fourth-smallest sovereign nation's government, a symbol of Tuvalu's resilience and low-lying island identity.
Funafuti Marine Conservation Area Vaiaku Islet
Home to the tiny capital's main settlement, this islet blends government buildings, guesthouses, and village life all within a short stroll of the lagoon shore.
Tuvalu National Library and Archives
A small but meaningful cultural institution preserving Tuvaluan history, oral traditions, and colonial-era records for this remote Pacific nation.
Funafuti Te Ano Beach and Foreshore
A picturesque stretch of white sand and calm shallows along the ocean side of Fongafale, popular for evening walks, fishing, and watching local games of te ano.

train.note: There are no railways in Tuvalu. Funafuti is reached by air on the Fiji Airways service from Suva, which operates only a few times a week - the runway doubles as a community space between flights. There is no rail anywhere in the country.

bus.note: No international coaches and no public bus service. Funafuti's single road runs about 12 km along the atoll, and almost everyone gets around by motorbike or on foot; a few pickup trucks act as informal taxis. There is no terminal.

intl.to: Outer islands - Nanumea, Nui, Vaitupu & Nukufetau (Tuvalu) - government vessels, a few times a month
intl.op: Tuvalu Maritime Services — tickets at the Funafuti wharf

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry - the only way in and out of the country is the Fiji flight. The government ships to the outer islands sail every few weeks on schedules announced locally, taking a day or more each way with basic deck accommodation. Small boats cross Funafuti lagoon to Funafala and the conservation area.

half.name: Funafala Islet
half.blurb: Small inhabited islet south of Fongafale reached by a thirty-minute boat ride, home to just a handful of families.
